text:
Johannes remained standing with the letter in his hand. Victoria was
dead. Again and again he spoke her name aloud, and his
voice was numb, almost hardened. He looked down at
the letter and recognized the handwriting; there were capital and lowercase letters,
the lines straight, and she who had written them was dead!

Then he makes his way in through his gate, up the stairs, finds
the right key to put into the lock, and opens the door. His room
was cold and dark. He sits down by the window and, in
the last remnant of daylight, reads Victoria’s letter.

Dear Johannes! she wrote. When you read this letter, I am
dead! Everything is so strange to me now; I am no longer ashamed
before you and am writing to you again, as though there were
nothing to prevent it. Before, while I was fully
alive, I would rather have suffered night and day than have written to
you again; but now my soul has begun to leave me, and I no longer
think that way. Strangers have seen me bleed, the doctor has
examined me and seen that I have only a remnant of one lung
left; what more have I to be ashamed of?

I have lain here on the bed and thought about the last words
I said to you. It was in the woods that evening. At the time I did
not think they would be my last words, for then I would have
said farewell to you at once and thanked you. Now I shall
never see you again, so now I regret that I did not throw
myself down before you and kiss your shoes and the ground you walked
on, and show you how inexpressibly I have loved you. I have
lain here both yesterday and today wishing that I were no sicker
than to be able to make my way home again and walk into the woods and
find the place where we sat when you held both my hands;
for then I could lie down there and see whether I could find
your traces and kiss all the heather around it. But I cannot
come home now unless perhaps I get a little better,
as Mama believes.

Dear Johannes! It is strange to think that I have
done nothing other than come into the world and
love you, and now say farewell to life. You may believe it is strange
to lie here and wait for the day and the hour. Step by step
I am moving away from life and the people in the street and the clatter
of carriages; I shall probably never see spring again either, and these
houses and the streets and the trees in the park will remain after me.
Today I was able to sit up in bed and look out of the window for a while. Down
on the corner there were two people who met; they greeted each other and clasped
each other’s hands and laughed at what they said; but then it was so strange
to me that I, who lay there watching this, was going to die. I found
myself thinking: those two down there do not know that I am lying here waiting
for my hour; but if they knew, they would probably still greet
each other and talk to each other just as they do now. Last night, when
it was dark, I thought it was going to be my final moment;
my heart began to stop, and it was as though I could already
hear eternity roaring toward me from far out. But in the next moment
I returned from far away and began to breathe again.
It was an utterly indescribable sensation. But Mama thinks that
perhaps it was only the river and the waterfall back home that I remembered.

Dear God, if only you knew how I have loved you,
Johannes. I have not been able to show you; so much has
stood in my way, first and foremost my own nature.
Papa too was so cruel to himself, and I am his daughter.
But now, when I am going to die and everything is too late, I am writing
to you once again and telling you so. I ask myself
why I am doing it, since it is nevertheless of no concern to you, especially
when I shall not even be alive anymore; but I should like
to be close to you until the end, so that at least I would not feel
more forsaken than before. When you read this, it is as though
I can see your shoulders and hands and see all your movements
with the letter as you hold it before you and read it. Then we
are not so far apart, I think. I cannot send for
you; I have no right to do so. Mama wanted to send for
you two days ago already, but I preferred to write. I also wanted most of all
for you to remember me as I once was, when I had not yet
been ill. I remember that you .... (Here some words have been omitted) .... my eyes and
eyebrows; but they too are no longer as they were before. For that
reason as well, I did not want you to come. And I shall also ask
you not to see me in my coffin. I shall presumably look much as
I did when I was alive, only somewhat paler, and I shall be lying in a yellow dress; but
nevertheless you would regret it if you came and saw me.

Now I have written on this letter many times today, and
even so I have not managed to tell you a thousandth of what I
wanted to say. It is so terrible for me to die; I do not want to;
I still hope so fervently in God that perhaps I might
get a little better, if only until spring. Then the days
are bright and there are leaves on the trees. If I were to recover now, I would
certainly never be unkind to you again, Johannes.
How I have wept and thought about it! Oh, I would go out and pat
all the paving stones and stop and thank every step in the stairways
I passed and be good to everyone. It would not matter how
much pain I suffered if only I were allowed to live. I would never complain
about anything again; no, I would smile at anyone who attacked
and struck me, and thank and praise God if I were allowed to live. My
life is so unlived; I have done nothing for anyone, and this
failed life is to end now. If you knew how loath I am to die,
then perhaps you would do something, do everything in your power.
You presumably cannot do anything; but I thought that if you and
the whole world prayed for me and would not let me go, then God
would grant me life. Oh, how grateful I would be then, and
never do wrong to anyone again, but smile at everything that was
ordained for me, if only I were allowed to live.

Mama is sitting here and weeping. She also sat here all night and
wept for me. This does me a little good; it softens the bitterness of my
farewell. Today I also thought: I wonder what you would think
if one day I came right up to you in the street, when I was nicely
dressed, and said nothing hurtful anymore, but gave you a rose
that I could have bought beforehand. Then immediately afterward I thought
that I can never again do what I want; for surely I can never
recover before I die. I weep so often; I lie quietly and
weep incessantly and inconsolably; it does not hurt in my chest when
I do not sob. Johannes, dear, dear friend, my only beloved
on earth, come to me now and stay here for a while when it begins
to grow dark. I shall not weep then, but smile as well as I
can, merely from joy that you came.
